title: Perfume, Palms and a Falling Seed
overview: As his final week begins, Jesus is honored at a dinner and cheered into Jerusalem, then speaks openly about his coming death and the mixed response to him.

parts.label: Mary's costly perfume (vv. 1-8)
parts.note: At a dinner in Bethany, Mary pours perfume worth about a year's pay on Jesus' feet and wipes them with her hair, a lavish act of love and humility. Jesus defends her against Judas, who the writer says was stealing from the group's money, and links the perfume to his coming burial, since bodies were prepared with spices.

parts.label: Lazarus and the king's arrival (vv. 9-19)
parts.note: News of Lazarus alive draws crowds, so the leaders plot to kill him too, and the next day people greet Jesus with palm branches, a sign of national celebration, and 'Hosanna', a cry meaning 'save us' that had become praise. Jesus rides a young donkey, echoing the prophet Zechariah's picture of a humble king who comes in peace rather than on a warhorse.

parts.label: Greeks and the wheat seed (vv. 20-26)
parts.note: When Greeks, outsiders drawn to Israel's God, ask to see him, Jesus takes it as a sign that his 'hour' has come. A seed must be buried to produce a harvest, and Christians read this as his death bringing life to many, with followers asked to hold their own lives loosely in the same way.

parts.label: Troubled, yet lifted up (vv. 27-36)
parts.note: Jesus admits he is deeply troubled but does not ask to escape, and a voice from heaven answers him that some in the crowd hear only as thunder. 'Lifted up' means being raised on a cross, which puzzles people who expected the promised king, the Messiah, to live forever.

parts.label: Why many did not believe (vv. 37-43)
parts.note: The writer explains widespread disbelief with two passages from Isaiah, including the hard line that God blinded their eyes. Readers have long debated what that means, and the writer adds that some leaders did believe but kept quiet, fearing they would be shut out of the synagogue, the heart of their community life.

parts.label: Light, not condemnation (vv. 44-50)
parts.note: In his last public words in this Gospel, Jesus says that to see and trust him is to see and trust the God who sent him, and he calls himself a light for people in the dark. He says he came to save, not to condemn, yet his words will be the measure people face in the end.

disagreement: Christians differ on how to understand verses 37 to 40: some read them as God actively causing unbelief, while others read them as God confirming a refusal people had already chosen.
think: When have you seen something have to end or be let go before something new could grow from it?
